description: We are two software engineers, computer sciences student and mechanical engineer who love hard problems, but more than that, we love exploring what we don't know yet. We're building a space mission simulator for the NASA challenge that shows how Cislunar Freight Trail Infrastructure unlocks the off-planet economy.
summary:
Lighthouse on the Trail is a browser game in which players design a robotic outpost at the Moon’s south pole the way NASA designs missions, then watch it operate for one year.

Players choose a landing site, launcher, landing pad, power mast, battery, communications, data storage, ice-delivery system and instruments, while six resources (mass, power, budget, data, communications and time) react to every choice. Each design must pass four NASA-style reviews that check real constraints and explain any failure in plain language. 

The year is then simulated hour by hour and replayed on a map built from real NASA lunar data: LOLA elevation, Diviner cold-trap temperatures and permanent-shadow maps. 

A debrief scores the mission and shows what to improve. Every number in the game is listed with its source and labelled as NASA data, engineering reference or game rule, so players learn real trade-offs from facts they can check.
details:
What it does. The player runs one mission from concept to operations in 15–25 minutes. Four design stages (Concept, Landing, Power, Ice) each end in a review modelled on NASA’s life cycle: MCR, SRR, PDR and CDR. The reviews check real constraints: landing slope and Earth visibility, rocket-plume standoff and launch mass, battery margin through the longest lunar night, and heater power, route slope and power-link range into a 40 K crater. A failed review names the check, the reason and the fix. Then the outpost operates for 8,760 simulated hours. The year is replayed on the map beside live charts of battery, solar power, data memory, Earth link and water ice. A debrief gives a score, the cause of any failure and badges tied to NASA’s technology shortfalls.

Why there is no single right answer. Every choice moves several resources at once, and hovering a choice previews its effect before committing. Several quite different designs succeed; each obvious shortcut fails at the review that names it.

Real data. The map is drawn from NASA LOLA elevation models (120 m regionally, 5 m per pixel near three sites), Diviner maximum temperatures for cold traps, and LOLA-derived permanent-shadow and illumination maps. An “About & numbers” page lists every number in the game with its source and marks it as NASA data, engineering reference or game rule. An automated test fails the build if a number has no source.

Learning. Each stage opens with a question the player answers before the explanation is shown. Optional “Want to know more?” calculations let players try the engineers’ arithmetic. Three difficulty levels and a shared-screen team mode with four roles are included.

How it is built. TypeScript and "Vite", no server and no framework. A deterministic simulation engine separate from the interface. Canvas map, SVG charts. "Vitest" unit tests and Playwright browser tests. Python scripts turn the raw NASA files into under 4 MB of data shipped with the game. Deployed with GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/gennady73/space-mission-simulator
